Dialect. A regional or social variety of a language, distinguished by phonological, grammatical, and lexical differences from other varieties. Once dismissed as substandard speech, modern sociolinguistics recognizes dialects as linguistically legitimate systems that reflect identity, geography, and social position. No dialect is inherently superior. All are rule-governed variations of the same language. The boundary between dialect and language is political rather than linguistic. Mutual intelligibility is a spectrum, not a binary.

A dialect differs from a language chiefly in mutual intelligibility—speakers of different dialects can generally understand each other. Dialects include regional varieties shaped by geography and isolation like Southern American English, Cockney, and Sicilian Italian. They also include social dialects shaped by class, ethnicity, and community, like African American Vernacular English and working-class speech. William Labov's sociolinguistic research elevated dialects from stigmatized variants to proper objects of study.

Dialect research demonstrates that linguistic prestige is social, not inherent. Standard dialects have power because institutions endorse them. Dialects often carry social markers. A single word choice can signal a speaker's origin, class, or education level. They evolve across generations as speakers incorporate new features and adapt to social pressures. Dialects serve as markers of group identity and belonging. Speakers often code-switch between dialects depending on context.

Stigmatization of non-standard dialects reflects social hierarchies, not linguistic deficiency. All dialects are equally complex rule systems. Network effects matter. Speakers in close social networks maintain shared features, while weak ties and geographic mobility spread new variants. Youth and women often pioneer linguistic change within their communities, adopting new features that eventually spread more widely.
